Mouse
mous
n. (an unclean creeping thing; the plague-sign of the Philistines)
From Old English mus. The Hebrew akbar covers mouse, rat, and similar rodents. It appears in the law of clean and unclean, in Isaiah's indictment of secret cult meals, and in the strange episode of the golden mice sent back with the ark.

Biblical Definition

The mouse is named in the law among the creatures that defile: “These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind” (Leviticus 11:29). Isaiah then uses it to expose a cult whose adherents thought themselves holy: “They that sanctify themselves, and purify themselves in the gardens behind one tree in the midst, eating swine's flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together, saith the LORD” (Isaiah 66:17). The detail is devastating — these people are performing purification rituals while eating what God called unclean. Religion and rebellion in one act. The mouse appears again in Philistia, where the men of Ashdod, struck with a plague while the ark stood among them, send it home with a guilt offering: “Wherefore ye shall make images of your emerods, and images of your mice that mar the land; and ye shall give glory unto the God of Israel: peradventure he will lighten his hand from off you, and from off your gods, and from off your land” (1 Samuel 6:5). The law's general principle governs: “And every creeping thing that flieth is unclean unto you: they shall not be eaten” (Deuteronomy 14:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the mouse as a small animal of the genus Mus, inhabiting houses — the common domestic mouse.

expand to see more

MOUSE, n. plu. mice. [Sax. mus.] A small animal of the genus Mus, inhabiting houses. The name is also applied to many other species of the genus.

MOUSE, v.i. To catch mice. To watch for and catch, as a cat.

UNCLEAN, a. Not clean; foul; dirty; filthy. In the Jewish law, ceremonially impure; not cleansed by ritual practices.

CREEPING, ppr. Moving on the belly, or with the body near the ground; moving slowly.

ABOMINATION, n. In Scripture, that which is exceedingly hateful and detestable to God; particularly, idols and idolatrous practices.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 11:29 — "These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind,"

Isaiah 66:17 — "They that sanctify themselves, and purify themselves in the gardens behind one tree in the midst, eating swine's flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together, saith the LORD."

Deuteronomy 14:19 — "And every creeping thing that flieth is unclean unto you: they shall not be eaten."

Leviticus 11:20 — "All fowls that creep, going upon all four, shall be an abomination unto you."

Modern Corruption

The dietary law is cited to prove that Scripture's moral commands are arbitrary and expired, which mistakes the ceremonial for the moral and ignores who abolished the one.

expand to see more

The argument is familiar: Leviticus forbids mice and shellfish, no one keeps that, therefore no one need keep what Leviticus says about anything else. Reformed theology has answered this for four centuries with a distinction the New Testament itself draws. The ceremonial law — food, festival, sacrifice, purification — was a shadow of good things to come and is fulfilled and abrogated in Christ; the moral law, summarized in the Ten Commandments, binds all men always. It was Christ who purged all meats, and Peter who was told not to call common what God had cleansed. The dietary code did not lapse by neglect; it was closed by the One it pointed to.

Isaiah 66:17 remains pointed for the church rather than against it. The people described are not pagans. They sanctify themselves, they purify themselves, and they are in a garden shrine eating mice. Scrupulous religious observance running alongside a forbidden practice is not a contradiction the human heart finds difficult; it is the normal condition of hypocrisy, and it is one of the few sins Christ attacked by name and at length.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew akbar (H5909), a mouse or rat; sherets (H8318), a swarming or creeping thing; tame (H2931), unclean; shiqquts (H8251), an abomination.

expand to see more

Hebrew akbar (H5909) — a mouse; Leviticus 11:29, Isaiah 66:17, 1 Samuel 6.

Hebrew sherets (H8318) — a swarming thing; the class the mouse belongs to.

Hebrew tame (H2931) — ceremonially unclean; the verdict of Leviticus 11.

Hebrew shiqquts (H8251) — a detestable thing; the abomination of Isaiah 66:17.

Greek koinos (G2839) — common, unclean; Acts 10:15, what God hath cleansed.

Usage

"“The weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise” — named in the law by kind."

"“They that sanctify themselves…eating…the mouse” — ritual and rebellion in one act."

"“Images of your mice that mar the land” — a pagan guilt offering."
